extracted.intended_audience: trial judges, patent litigators, and jurors (users of AIPLA model patent jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for determining patent infringement and invalidity issues (including §271(f)(2), §271(g), prior art, anticipation, public use, on-sale bar, printed publications, experimental use, and prior invention) in U.S. patent litigation. Intended as draftable instructions and explanatory guidance for use at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(f)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] asserts that [the Defendant] infringed a claim ... by supplying [or causing to be supplied] [a component][components] of a claimed invention ... from the United States into a foreign country, where the exported component[s] [was][were] especially made or especially adapted for use in an invention covered by the [patent] and [has][have] no substantial non-infringing use[s], and where [the Defendant] knew the component[s] [was][were] especially made or adapted for use in the claimed invention and intended for the component[s] to be combined in a way that would have infringed the [patent] if the combination had occurred in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show infringement under Section 271(f)(2), [the Plaintiff] must prove that each of the following is more likely than not: (1) [the Defendant] actually supplied the components from the United States into a foreign country or caused them to be supplied; (2) [the Defendant] knew or should have known that the components were especially made or adapted for use in a product that infringes a claim of the patent; (3) those components have no substantial non-infringing use; and (4) [the Defendant] intended for the components to be combined into that product. It is not necessary to find that the components actually were combined into an infringing product, only that the defendant intended the combination to be made such that it would have infringed if in the U.S. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §271(f)(2); Cardiac Pacemakers v. St. Jude; Microsoft v. AT&T; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by import/sale/offer/use of product made by patented process (§271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: [Plaintiff] asserts that [Defendant] infringed ... by [importing][selling][offering for sale][using] a product that was made by a process covered by one or more claims of the [patent].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show infringement under Section 271(g), [Plaintiff] must prove more likely than not: (1) [Defendant] [imported/sold/offered/used] a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the patent; (2) the product was made between [issue date] and [expiration date or date of trial]; and (3) the defendant [imported/sold/offered/used] the product between those dates. If the product was materially changed by later processes, or is only a trivial or non-essential part of another product, it was not “made by” the claimed process. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §271(g); Amgen v. F. Hoffman-La Roche; Mycogen v. Monsanto; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] must prove that it is highly probable that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This burden of proof on the defendant never changes regardless of whether the Patent Examiner considered the reference. The instruction uses the phrasing 'highly probable' to describe the defendant's burden in proving invalidity. (Citations: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin; Group One v. Hallmark.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (pre-AIA) — what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes items received into evidence: any [product/method] publicly known or used by others in the United States before the claimed invention was invented; any [product/method] that was in public use or on sale in the United States before [Cutoff Date]; any patents that issued before [Cutoff Date]; any publications having dates of public accessibility before [Cutoff Date]; and any [product/method] made by anyone in the United States before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-AIA definitions when applicable. Identify the prior art admitted into evidence and any disputed issues (dates, public availability) to the jury. (Citation: 35 U.S.C. §102 (pre-AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art (AIA) — what counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes: (1) anything patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of the claim(s); and (2) anything described in a patent or patent application published or deemed published, naming another inventor and filed before the effective filing date of the claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use AIA §102 definitions when applicable. Identify references the defendant contends are prior art. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102 as amended by the AIA; 35 U.S.C. §100(i).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to prior art (AIA) — disclosures by/inventor and ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions: (1) A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date is not prior art if the disclosure was made by the inventor/joint inventor or obtained directly/indirectly from such inventor; and (2) a disclosure is not prior art if the subject matter was obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor, had been publicly disclosed earlier by the inventor or one who derived it from the inventor, or the subject matter and claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues exist (e.g., whether a disclosure was within one year or was derived from the inventor), instruct the jury on the appropriate exceptions under §102(b) and (c) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art considered or not considered by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner during prosecution, [the Defendant] must prove that it is highly probable that the challenged claim(s) is/are invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defendant's burden remains the same even if the Examiner did or did not consider a reference. (Citations: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin; SIBIA Neurosciences v. Cadus; Group One v. Hallmark.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of independent and dependent claims — separate evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two types of claims: independent and dependent. An independent claim does not refer to any other claim. A dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements of the claim to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must evaluate the invalidity of each asserted claim separately. Even if an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims that depend from it are not automatically invalid — each claim must be considered separately. However, if you find a dependent claim invalid, then you must find the independent claim from which it depends invalid as well because the dependent claim includes all elements of the independent claim. (Citations: Comaper v. Antec; Callaway v. Acushnet; Ormco v. Align Tech.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the [time of the invention/effective filing date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art must be evaluated from the perspective of that person of ordinary skill as of the relevant date. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §103; KSR v. Teleflex; Continental Can v. Monsanto.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) — single-reference requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim. You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In determining whether every element is found in the prior publication/patent/etc., consider what a person of ordinary skill would have understood from review of that reference. If inherency is alleged, instruct the jury on inherency. (Citations: NetMoneyIN v. Verisign; Toro v. Deere; Schering v. Geneva.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art inherently anticipates a patent claim if the missing element or feature would necessarily result from what the single item of prior art teaches to persons of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party claiming inherent anticipation must prove it is highly probable that the allegedly inherent element necessarily is present. Evidence outside the prior art reference (including experimental testing) may be used to show inherent elements. To be inherent, the feature must necessarily have existed — likelihood is not sufficient. It is not required that persons of ordinary skill recognized the inherent disclosure at the time. (Practice note: instruct jury on inherency if alleged.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (pre-AIA) — criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was publicly known by others in the United States before [§102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That claim is invalid if the invention was publicly known by others in the U.S. before it was invented by the patentee. If date of invention or priority date is disputed, instruct jury how to determine Cutoff Date. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a) (pre-AIA); Minnesota Mining v. Chemque; Ecolochem v. S. Cal. Edison.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public knowledge (AIA) — criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the claimed invention was available to the public before [§102(a) (AIA) Cutoff Date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That claim is invalid if the claimed invention was available to the public before the effective filing date. If factual issues as to disclosures within one year, exceptions under §102(b) and (c) should be instructed. (Citation: 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (pre-AIA) — definition and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was publicly used by others in the United States before [Cutoff Date] (or more than one year before the patentee filed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The patent claim is invalid if the invention was publicly used in the U.S. The invention was publicly used if an embodiment was both (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the U.S., and (2) ready for patenting. Factors relevant: nature of the activity, public access to the use, confidentiality obligations imposed on observers, commercial exploitation, circumstances of testing/experimentation. Absence of steps to conceal is evidence of public use; secret use by third party is not public unless members/employees had access. If date of invention is disputed, instruct jury on Cutoff Date. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) (pre-AIA); Clock Spring; Invitrogen; Netscape.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use (AIA) — definition and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before the effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent claim is invalid if claimed invention was in public use anywhere before the effective filing date. Factors relevant are same as pre-AIA (nature of activity, public access, confidentiality, commercial exploitation, testing). An invention is publicly used if used by inventor or by someone not under secrecy obligation. (Citation: 35 U.S.C. §102(a)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready for patenting / Reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is ready for patenting when there is reason to believe it would work for its intended purpose. It is ready when (1) reduced to practice, or (2) inventor has prepared drawings/descriptions sufficient to allow a person of ordinary skill to make or use the invention. An invention is reduced to practice when (1) constructed or performed within scope of the patent claims, and (2) determined that it works for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'ready for patenting' standard applies to public use and on-sale bar analyses. (Citations: Cooper v. Goldfarb; Grain Processing; Moleculon Research.)

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was on sale (pre-AIA: in the United States) before the cutoff date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That claim is invalid if before the cutoff an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale (pre-AIA: in the U.S.), and (2) ready for patenting. A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by accepting the offer. The essential question is whether a product embodying the invention was commercially marketed; an actual sale is not required. If issues about disclosures within one year or common ownership exist under AIA, instruct on §102(b)/(c) exceptions. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(b) (pre-AIA); Pfaff v. Wells Elecs.; Medicines Co. v. Hospira.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] contends that __ should not be considered a prior public use or placing the invention on sale because that use/sale was experimental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities are experimental if a legitimate effort to test claimed features or determine if invention works for intended purpose; primary purpose must be experimentation. Only experimentation by or under control of the inventor (or assignee) qualifies; experimentation by a third party for its own purposes does not. Experimentation must relate to claimed features and technological improvement, not commercial exploitation; incidental profit is permissible. A test done primarily for marketing is not experimental. If defendant shows it is highly probable there was a prior public use/sale, burden shifts to plaintiff to show experimental purpose and, if convincing, the jury may find no prior public use/sale. (Citations: City of Elizabeth v. Nicholson Pavement; Clock Spring; Lisle; Allen Eng'g; LaBounty.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication — accessibility and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was described in a printed publication before the relevant cutoff date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A printed publication must have been maintained in tangible form (printed pages, electronic file, microfilm, photos, Internet publication, photocopies) and sufficiently accessible to persons interested and ordinarily skilled. Disclosure must be complete enough to enable one of ordinary skill to use the invention without undue experimentation. Information is publicly accessible if distributed or otherwise made available such that persons interested and of ordinary skill exercising reasonable diligence can locate it. Issued patents and published patent applications are printed publications. If accessibility is disputed, give additional instruction on accessibility. (Citations: 35 U.S.C. §102(a),(b) pre-AIA; §102(a)(1),(a)(2) AIA; In re NTP; In re Lister; Kyocera Wireless.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention (pre-AIA) — earlier inventor defense
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must show it is highly probable that (1) before the patentee invented it, the third party reduced to practice a product/method that included all features of the claim, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in reducing the invention to practice. The prior invention must be sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work. This defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. If priority of invention is submitted to the jury, additional instructions on conception and reduction to practice and diligence are required. (Practice note and citations provided.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, suppression, or concealment of a prior invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed, it does not anticipate the patent-in-suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may find a prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed if it is highly probable that (1) the prior inventor actively concealed the invention from the public, or (2) the prior inventor unreasonably delayed making the invention publicly known. Generally, a prior invention was not abandoned/suppressed/concealed if it was made public, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used commercially. A period of delay does not constitute abandonment if the prior inventor was engaged in reasonable efforts to bring the invention to market. If this issue is asserted, define the terms for the jury as appropriate. (Citations: Dow Chem. Co. v. Astro-Valcour; Checkpoint Sys. v. U.S. ITC.)
